content.title: About
content.content: A whole wheat bagel with raisins is a ring‑shaped baked good made from whole‑grain wheat flour. Dried raisins are folded into the dough, giving the bagel a subtle sweetness and a pleasant aroma. The result is a dense, slightly chewy crust with a soft, flavorful interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bagels originated in the Jewish communities of Eastern Europe and were traditionally boiled before baking.
Whole wheat flour retains the bran and germ, making the bagel more nutritious than a standard white‑flour version.
Raisins not only add sweetness but also help retain moisture, keeping the crumb tender after cooling.
Boiling the dough in water with a touch of baking soda or honey creates the characteristic glossy, firm crust.
In many countries the bagel is considered a “grab‑and‑go” breakfast because it is easy to eat on the move.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole wheat flour provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs deliver sustained energy and promote a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are essential for oxygen transport and muscle function.

items.title: Natural antioxidants from raisins
items.content: Raisins are rich in polyphenols, which help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When baked without hydrogenated oils, the bagel remains a healthier alternative to many processed pastries.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made with wheat flour, this bagel contains gluten and may trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins add natural sugars; individuals monitoring blood glucose should account for this.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Bagels are relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the bagel and spread cream cheese, hummus, or nut butter. It pairs well with fresh vegetables, avocado, or smoked salmon. For a sweeter option, toast and drizzle with honey or jam.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the bagel in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Warm in a toaster or oven before serving to restore the crisp crust.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-dry-mix-reduced-suga.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, dry mix, reduced sugar, made with water

content.title: About
content.content: The dry mix for hot chocolate/cocoa with reduced sugar is designed to be prepared with water. It contains cocoa powder, a sweetener, salt and flavorings. When mixed with hot water it yields a rich chocolate drink with moderate sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix is created for those who want to cut sugar intake without giving up the taste of hot chocolate.
The cocoa powder is enriched with antioxidants such as flavonoids.
Dry mixes are shelf‑stable and keep their flavor for up to 12 months.
Preparation takes 1–2 minutes: simply pour 200 ml of hot water and stir.
Often used in offices and schools where milk is not readily available.

items.title: Rich in flavonoids
items.content: Flavonoids in cocoa have antioxidant properties that support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Reduced sugar intake
items.content: Compared with regular mixes, this version contains roughly half the sugar.

items.title: Mood support
items.content: Cocoa stimulates the production of serotonin and endorphins, which can improve mood.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Prepared with water, the drink is less caloric and suitable for weight‑conscious individuals.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: The mix provides magnesium and iron, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to cocoa or the added flavorings.

items.title: Caffeine content
items.content: Cocoa contains a small amount of caffeine; caffeine‑sensitive people should take this into account.

items.title: Artificial sweetener
items.content: The reduced‑sugar version uses a non‑nutritive sweetener, which may not be suitable for certain dietary restrictions.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Pour 200 ml of boiling water into a cup, add 2 packets (≈20 g) of the dry mix, and stir thoroughly until smooth. Optional additions include milk, cream, or spices such as cinnamon or vanilla.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3–6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Meat spread (potted meat) NFS is a ready‑to‑eat product made from selected beef and pork, seasoned with spices and a modest amount of fat. It is packed in a sealed can, providing a long shelf life without refrigeration.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “potted meat” originates from the English tradition of preserving meat in clay pots with added fat for extended storage.
NFS uses a technology that retains up to 90 % of the original protein content.
The product is popular among hikers and in situations with limited access to fresh food.
Small pieces of vegetables such as carrot or onion may be included to enhance flavor.
A typical can weighs 200 g and has a shelf life of 2–5 years.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Meat spread provides about 15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat in the spread is rich in heme iron, which is readily absorbed.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product contains vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: The sealed packaging allows consumption without cooking, ideal for field conditions.

items.title: Low carbohydrate
items.content: Meat spread contains virtually no carbs, making it suitable for low‑carb diets.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salt is added for flavor and preservation; people with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The spread contains saturated fats, so it should be eaten in moderation, especially by those with cardiovascular concerns.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef or pork.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain batches may contain food additives (e.g., nitrites) to extend shelf life.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Meat spread can be eaten straight from the can, spread on bread, crackers, or toast. It can also be gently warmed in a microwave or skillet, adding extra spices if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the can in the refrigerator and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pancakes are nutritious flat cakes made from whole‑grain flour, eggs, milk and a small amount of oil. They have a soft texture, a mild nutty flavor, and retain most of the nutrients found in whole grains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain flour keeps the bran and germ, making the pancakes higher in fiber and vitamins than regular pancakes.
The batter can be customized with berries, nuts, protein powder or plant‑based milk for different dietary needs.
While traditionally cooked on a skillet, they can also be baked in the oven for an even rise.
In many countries they are served with maple syrup, yogurt or fresh fruit.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides soluble and insoluble fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: These pancakes supply thiamine, niacin and folate, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Compared with white‑flour pancakes, whole‑grain versions cause a slower rise in blood sugar.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Combined with eggs and milk, they deliver a complete amino‑acid profile useful for muscle repair.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Magnesium, iron and zinc in the pancakes support muscle function, immunity and metabolic processes.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole‑grain flour contains gluten, so people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should choose gluten‑free alternatives.

items.title: Added sugar in toppings
items.content: Pancakes are often served with sweet syrups; excess sugar can offset their nutritional benefits.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although more nutritious, they still provide calories, so portion control is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pancakes with berries, nuts, low‑fat yogurt, honey or avocado. They work well as a base for savory wraps with vegetables and lean cheese, or can be frozen in portions for a quick breakfast.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pancakes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in bags, separating portions; reheat in the microwave or on a skillet before serving.

pizza-with-meat-other-than-pepperoni-fro.title: Pizza with meat other than pepperoni, medium crust

content.title: About
content.content: This is a pizza made in a restaurant or fast‑food outlet, topped with assorted meats (such as ham, beef, chicken or sausage) but without pepperoni. The medium‑thick crust (category 3412) provides a balance between a crisp edge and a soft interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat‑topped pizzas often combine several types of meat to create a more complex flavor profile.
Medium crust is typically baked at 220‑250 °C for about 10‑12 minutes.
In Italy, meat pizzas are traditionally called “pizza with salami” or “pizza with ham,” but fast‑food versions frequently add chicken and beef.
The classic combination of tomato sauce, mozzarella cheese, and meat toppings is considered well‑balanced.
Meat pizzas are often served with extra sauces such as garlic, barbecue, or hot sauce.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Meat and cheese provide a high amount of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat and sausage contain heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and tomato sauce are good sources of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Mozzarella adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The medium crust and meat toppings provide a quick source of energy, useful for active lifestyles.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Meat‑topped pizza can be calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Saturated fat and sodium
items.content: Sausages and cheese contain saturated fats and salt, which may affect cholesterol and blood pressure.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should choose dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked meat can harbor pathogens; ensure the pizza is fully cooked.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pizza into bite‑size pieces and enjoy it hot while the cheese is still stretchy. Add fresh vegetables, arugula, or basil for extra freshness. Serve with chili sauce, garlic aioli, or a drizzle of olive oil if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness; a microwave will make the crust soggy.

content.title: About
content.content: Ruffled potato chips with barbecue flavor are thinly sliced potatoes fried until crisp and coated with a smoky, sweet‑spicy seasoning blend typical of barbecue: smoked pepper, paprika, onion and garlic.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The ruffled shape increases surface area, allowing the seasoning to cling better.
Barbecue flavor originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a way to mimic smoked meat aromas.
Potato chips became a popular snack in 1853 after the invention of a mechanical slicer.
There are over 200 chip flavors worldwide, with barbecue consistently ranking in the top five.
Most manufacturers use a polyphosphate solution to preserve crunchiness.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Chips provide carbohydrates that quickly supply the body with energy.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: Despite frying, a small amount of vitamin C remains in the potato.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Potassium and iron are present, supporting muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Antioxidants in spices
items.content: Paprika and smoked pepper contain carotenoids with antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Chips often contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure when eaten frequently.

items.title: Fats and calories
items.content: Deep‑frying makes the product calorie‑dense and rich in saturated and trans fats.

items.title: Allergy to potato or spices
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to potato or added flavorings.

items.title: Acrylamide
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound, so moderation is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy chips as a standalone snack, toss them into salads, use as a crunchy topping for soups, or incorporate into party appetizers. Opt for lower‑salt versions when possible.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in a sealed package in a cool, dry place away from light. After opening, transfer to an airtight container to maintain crispness.
